paper.title: Notes on Catalytic P Systems
paper.abstract: In this paper we address the possibility of studying the computational capabilities of catalytic P systems with one catalyst by the means of iterated finite state transducers (IFT). In particular, we focus on a variant of catalytic P systems which satisfies in addition to the original definition the following property: if in a region of the P system an object is the subject of a catalytic rule, then in the same region it must exists also a non-cooperative rule that rewrites the same object. Finally, we also give a normal form for catalytic P systems.

verdict.summary: Short computability-theory note giving a normal form for catalytic P systems and an inclusion of mixed one-catalyst P systems in the length sets of 3-state iterated finite transducers; formalism is the native language of the subject and proportionate, though the proofs are sketched rather than complete.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Computational power of catalytic P systems (membrane computing). The paper proves a Chomsky-style normal form for catalytic P systems (Theorem 1) and shows that mixed catalytic P systems with one catalyst generate only length sets of languages produced by iterated finite state transducers with three states (Theorem 2, Corollary 3), recasting the open question of one-catalyst universality as a question about IFTs.
**Level:** 4 (High)
**Rationale:** The contribution consists of computability results proved by simulation constructions in formal language theory. It does not prove universality or undecidability (which would place it at Level 5), and per the default-lower rule it is placed at Level 4 as a paper proving computational-power (family inclusion) results.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 5 (IFT and its derivation relation, catalytic P system, mixed P system, configuration/computation semantics, the families NOP_m([M]cat_k) and N_{O-C}P_m)
- Theorems: 3 (Theorem 1, Theorem 2, Corollary 3)
- Proofs: 2
- Equations: the rule schemes (1)-(3), the extended alphabet O', the partition sets X, Y, T and the transducer components K, V, F

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 5x2 + 3x3 + 2x4 = 27
Expected range (Level 4): 30-80
Ratio: 0.34x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. Every definition is used in the statements or proofs of the theorems. Set notation (the partition O = X ∪ Y ∪ T ∪ {c}, the alphabet extension, families of length sets) is the subject matter of formal language theory, not notation standing in for programming operations, so the Necessity Test is passed throughout.

### Issues
- The proof of Theorem 1 refers to "Section ??", a broken cross-reference, for the reduction to one membrane; the result is in fact cited from [7] in Section 2.2.
- The proof of Theorem 1 gives only the rules simulating non-cooperative rules; the catalytic case is dismissed as "defined similarly", and the delay chain is defined only for rules with at least two right-hand-side symbols.
- The proof of Theorem 2 argues the forward simulation informally and asserts a bijective correspondence between configurations and processed strings without proving the converse direction (that every accepted IFT derivation corresponds to a halting computation). Theorem 2 is also stated for N OP_1 while the construction counts objects of O \ {c}, i.e. the N_{O-C} variant.
- Remark 4.1 contains two conjectures and an explicitly stated open problem; these are honestly labelled as such.

---

## Citation Analysis

Seven references, one self-citation ([7], Sburlan 2006 on P systems with promoters/inhibitors), giving SCR = 1/7 = 14.3%, within the normal band. The self-citation is used for the known result that catalytic P systems can be reduced to one membrane, which the normal-form proof relies on, so it is topically related (similarity well above 0.5). The other references are the foundational works of the field (Păun's introduction of P systems, the two-catalyst universality result, the IFT hierarchy of Bordihn et al.). References [4] and [5] are listed but not cited in the text. No concerning patterns.

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are supported by proofs or by citation of established results; the conclusion does not overstate what was proved and frames the one-catalyst question as still open. Limitations are acknowledged inline through the conjectures and the explicit open problem in Remark 4.1, though there is no dedicated limitations section. The sketchiness of both proofs and the broken cross-reference weaken the structure. As a pure theory paper it has nothing to release; no artifact is linked or claimed.

---

## Conclusion

A brief, legitimate theoretical note in membrane computing whose formal apparatus is proportionate to, and required by, its computability results. No formalism, citation, or structural flags apply. Its main weaknesses are proofs presented at sketch level (one case of Theorem 1 omitted, the converse direction of Theorem 2 asserted rather than proved) and editorial slips such as the unresolved section reference. No instructions addressed to a reviewer or analyst were found in the paper text.
